recipes.name: Petrolatum Cold Cream
recipes.description: A simple cold cream built on a petrolatum and lanolin base. Easier to make and more shelf-stable than the spermaceti-based historic cold creams. Works as a heavy moisturizer or as the oil-phase of a wipe-off makeup cleanser.
recipes.notes: Melt the paraffin, then add the lanolin and petrolatum. When all are melted, transfer to a warm mortar and slowly incorporate the water with constant stirring. When the cream is nearly cold, add the essential oil and a small amount of optional borax dissolved in alcohol. Original adds 'a small quantity of borax may be added, if desirable.'

attribution.displayName: Henley's Twentieth Century Book of Recipes, Formulas and Processes (1907 / 1914 ed.)
attribution.author: Gardner D. Hiscox (ed.)
attribution.originalSource: Henley's Twentieth Century Book of Recipes, Formulas and Processes — COSMETICS section, 'Petrolatum Cold Cream'
attribution.originalRecipe: Petrolatum Cold Cream.— Petrolatum (white) 7 ounces; Paraffine 1/2 ounce; Lanolin 2 ounces; Water 3 ounces; Oil of rose 3 drops; Alcohol 1 drachm. A small quantity of borax may be added, if desirable, and the perfume may be varied to suit the taste.
attribution.notes: Percentages are approximate conversions from apothecary weights; verify before production. Original published 1907 (Hiscox died 1908), digitized 1914 edition on Project Gutenberg. PD by 95-year publication rule (any work published before 1930 is PD in 2026).

recipes.name: Tragacanth Cold Cream
recipes.description: A lighter gel-based cold cream using tragacanth gum as the thickener. No animal fats, no spermaceti — closer in feel to a modern lightweight gel moisturizer than to the rich Victorian cold creams.
recipes.notes: Mix the tragacanth and the boric acid with the glycerin; add the almond oil, lavender oil, and egg glycerite (glyconine), which have been previously well incorporated, and lastly add the water in divided portions until a clear jelly of the desired consistency is obtained. Note: 'glyconine' (egg yolk + glycerin) is a historic ingredient — modern substitution would be a small amount of lecithin or an emulsifier.

attribution.displayName: Henley's Twentieth Century Book of Recipes, Formulas and Processes (1907 / 1914 ed.)
attribution.author: Gardner D. Hiscox (ed.)
attribution.originalSource: Henley's Twentieth Century Book of Recipes — COSMETICS section, 'Cold Cream II'
attribution.originalRecipe: II.— Tragacanth 125 parts; Boric acid 100 parts; Glycerine 140 parts; Expressed oil of almonds 50 parts; Glyconine 50 parts; Oil of lavender 0.5 parts; Water enough to make 1,000 parts. Mix the tragacanth and the boric acid with the glycerine; add the almond oil, lavender oil, and egg glycerite, which have been previously well incorporated, and, lastly, add the water in divided portions until a clear jelly of the desired consistency is obtained.
attribution.notes: Percentages are direct conversions from parts (1000 = 100%). Glyconine = egg-yolk glycerite, historic emulsifier. Boric acid at 10% is HIGH by modern standards (regulatory limits suggest <5%) — recommend reducing before production. Modern substitution: replace with a small amount of cosmetic-grade emulsifier.

recipes.name: Lipol — Lip Salve for Chapped Lips
recipes.description: A medicated lip balm with camphor, menthol, and eucalyptus for relief of sore, rough, or inflamed lips. Alkanet root tints the salve a soft red; substituting mica or cosmetic-safe glitter for the alkanet creates a sparkly variant.

ingredients.name: Alkanet Root (for color, infused into oil phase)

recipes.notes: Digest the alkanet root in the melted paraffin and petrolatum, strain to remove the root, then add the camphor, menthol, eucalyptol, and essential oils. Pour into lip jars while hot. Apply night and morning, rubbing in well with the finger tips. SPARKLY VARIANT: replace alkanet with cosmetic-grade mica (e.g., 0.5-1% by weight) for shimmer; mica does not need to be infused — stir in during the final pour. Safety note: bitter almond oil contains traces of benzaldehyde-derived compounds; modern formulators may prefer pure benzaldehyde-free oil or a safer flavor.

attribution.displayName: Henley's Twentieth Century Book of Recipes, Formulas and Processes (1907 / 1914 ed.)
attribution.author: Gardner D. Hiscox (ed.)
attribution.originalSource: Henley's Twentieth Century Book of Recipes — COSMETICS section, 'Lipol'
attribution.originalRecipe: Lipol.—For treating sore, rough, or inflamed lips, apply the following night and morning, rubbing in well with the finger tips: Camphor, 1/2 ounce; menthol, 1/2 ounce; eucalyptol, 1 drachm; petrolatum (white), 1 pound; paraffine, 1/2 pound; alkanet root, 1/2 ounce; oil of bitter almonds, 15 drops; oil of cloves, 10 drops; oil of cassia, 5 drops. Digest the root in the melted paraffine and petrolatum, strain, add the other ingredients and pour into lip jars, hot.
attribution.notes: This is the closest historic analog to a modern sparkly lip gloss base — swap alkanet (red plant tint) for mica or cosmetic glitter for shimmer. Camphor + menthol at this concentration is intentionally medicinal; reduce for non-medicinal cosmetic use.

recipes.name: Effervescent Bath Tablets
recipes.description: The historic ancestor of the modern bath bomb. Tartaric acid + sodium bicarbonate produces a copious effervescence in bathwater; rice flour acts as binder. Can be used as loose powder (a few spoonfuls per tub) or compressed into tablets.
recipes.notes: Mix the dry ingredients thoroughly. Compress into tablets, moistening with alcohol if necessary (NEVER water — water triggers the effervescent reaction immediately). For perfume, add essential oils at about 1 fluidrachm per pound of powder (roughly 0.8% by weight). Original mentions oil of lavender alone, or a 1:6 rose geranium / lavender blend, or full Cologne-water oil blend (lavender + rosemary + bergamot + lemon + clove). MODERN ADAPTATION: most modern bath bombs use citric acid instead of tartaric acid at similar ratios; tartaric acid works too and is what the 1907 source specifies.

attribution.displayName: Henley's Twentieth Century Book of Recipes, Formulas and Processes (1907 / 1914 ed.)
attribution.author: Gardner D. Hiscox (ed.)
attribution.originalSource: Henley's Twentieth Century Book of Recipes — BATH TABLETS, EFFERVESCENT
attribution.originalRecipe: BATH TABLETS, EFFERVESCENT. Tartaric acid 10 parts; Sodium bicarbonate 9 parts; Rice flour 6 parts. A few spoonfuls of this, when stirred into a bathtubful of water, causes a copious liberation of carbon dioxide, which is refreshing. This mixture can be made into tablets by compression, moistening, if necessary, with alcohol. Water, of course, cannot be used in making them, as its presence causes the decomposition referred to. Perfume may be added to this powder, essential oils being a good form. Oil of lavender would be a suitable addition, in the proportion of a fluidrachm or more to the pound of powder.
attribution.notes: This is a genuine bath-bomb antecedent published in 1907 — Lush's commercial bath bomb (1989) uses an almost identical chemistry (citric acid + bicarb instead of tartaric + bicarb). For shimmer, add cosmetic-grade mica during dry mixing.

recipes.name: Hand Lotion (Boric Acid + Glycerin Base)
recipes.description: A simple anhydrous hand balm of lanolin and petroleum jelly with glycerin and boric acid for skin conditioning. Thick and protective — closer to a hand salve than a modern pump lotion.
recipes.notes: Dissolve the boric acid in the glycerin with gentle heat. Cool the glycerin mixture before combining with lanolin and petrolatum (do not add hot glycerin solution to fats). Add any perfume desired. SAFETY NOTE: boric acid at 2% is at the historic dosage but exceeds modern regulatory limits for some jurisdictions (EU restricts to 5% in cosmetics for adults, 0.1% for products that might be used on broken skin or children). Consider reducing.

attribution.displayName: Henley's Twentieth Century Book of Recipes, Formulas and Processes (1907 / 1914 ed.)
attribution.author: Gardner D. Hiscox (ed.)
attribution.originalSource: Henley's Twentieth Century Book of Recipes — COSMETICS section, 'Lotion For The Hands'
attribution.originalRecipe: Lotion For The Hands.— Boric acid 1 drachm; Glycerine 6 drachms; Dissolve by heat and mix with Lanolin 6 drachms; Vaseline 1 ounce. Add any perfume desired. The borated glycerine should be cooled before mixing it with the lanolin.
attribution.notes: Anhydrous — no water phase, so no preservative strictly required, but boric acid acts as a mild antimicrobial. Texture will be thick/balm-like, not pourable.

recipes.name: Cosmetic Jelly (Tragacanth + Rose Water)
recipes.description: A light skin jelly made by macerating tragacanth gum in rose water, with glycerin and alcohol added for body and preservation. Apply after bathing, rubbing in until dry.
recipes.notes: Macerate the tragacanth in the rose water for two days, then strain forcibly through coarse muslin or cheesecloth. Add the glycerin and alcohol. Perfume to suit (optional). Apply immediately after bathing, rubbing in well until dry. SAFETY NOTE: contains water — needs a preservative for shelf stability. Original 1907 source doesn't specify one; add a modern broad-spectrum preservative (e.g., Geogard Ultra at ~0.75-1%) for any batch intended to last more than a few days.

attribution.displayName: Henley's Twentieth Century Book of Recipes, Formulas and Processes (1907 / 1914 ed.)
attribution.author: Gardner D. Hiscox (ed.)
attribution.originalSource: Henley's Twentieth Century Book of Recipes — COSMETICS section, 'Cosmetic Jelly'
attribution.originalRecipe: Cosmetic Jelly.— Tragacanth (white ribbon) 60 grains; Rose water 14 ounces; Macerate for two days and strain forcibly through coarse muslin or cheese cloth. Add glycerine and alcohol, of each 1 ounce. Perfume to suit. Use immediately after bathing, rubbing in well until dry.
attribution.notes: Light texture — suitable as a hydrating after-bath gel or layered under heavier creams.

recipes.name: Massage Cream (Petrolatum + Lanolin Base)
recipes.description: A petrolatum-and-lanolin massage cream lightly emulsified with water, perfumed with rose and vanillin. Closer to a body butter than to a slip massage oil — works well for deep tissue or for nightly skin nourishment.
recipes.notes: Melt the paraffin, then add the lanolin and petrolatum. Once melted, pour into a warm mortar and, with constant stirring, slowly incorporate the water. When nearly cold, add the rose oil and vanillin dissolved in the alcohol. Original calls it 'Massage Skin Food III' and emphasizes vigorous rubbing into the skin: 'friction assists the absorbed fat in developing the muscles, and also imparts softness and fullness to the skin.'

attribution.displayName: Henley's Twentieth Century Book of Recipes, Formulas and Processes (1907 / 1914 ed.)
attribution.author: Gardner D. Hiscox (ed.)
attribution.originalSource: Henley's Twentieth Century Book of Recipes — COSMETICS section, 'Massage Skin Foods III'
attribution.originalRecipe: III.— White petrolatum 7 av. ounces; Paraffine wax 1/2 ounce; Lanolin 2 av. ounces; Water 3 fluidounces; Oil of rose 3 drops; Vanillin 2 grains; Alcohol 1 fluidrachm. Melt the paraffine, add the lanolin and petrolatum, and when these have melted pour the mixture into a warm mortar, and, with constant stirring, incorporate the water. When nearly cold add the oil and vanillin, dissolved in the alcohol.
attribution.notes: Same base as Petrolatum Cold Cream (pd-001) but with vanillin added — that's the only material difference. Recipe explicitly designed for massage friction.

recipes.name: Astringent Wash for Oily Skin (Cucumber + Benzoin)
recipes.description: A light astringent toner combining cucumber juice (hydrating + cooling), tincture of benzoin (antimicrobial resin), cologne, and elder-flower water. Closest historic analog to a modern micellar water or alcohol-based skin tonic.
recipes.notes: Put the tincture of benzoin in an 8-ounce bottle first, then add the other ingredients (previously mixed). Shake slightly. Some precipitation of benzoin will occur — it can be left to settle, or strained out through cheesecloth. Apply with sponge night and morning. Use for coarse pores, oily, or flabby skin. SHELF LIFE NOTE: fresh cucumber juice is the spoilage risk — make in small batches or substitute cucumber hydrosol for longer shelf life. The alcohol from the tincture and cologne provides some preservation.

attribution.displayName: Henley's Twentieth Century Book of Recipes, Formulas and Processes (1907 / 1914 ed.)
attribution.author: Gardner D. Hiscox (ed.)
attribution.originalSource: Henley's Twentieth Century Book of Recipes — COSMETICS section, 'Astringent Wash For Flabby Skin'
attribution.originalRecipe: Astringent Wash For Flabby Skin.—This is used to correct coarse pores, and to remedy an oily or flabby skin. Apply with sponge night and morning: Cucumber juice 1 1/2 ounces; Tincture of benzoin 1/2 ounce; Cologne 1 ounce; Elder-flower water 5 ounces. Put the tincture of benzoin in an 8-ounce bottle, add the other ingredients, previously mixed, and shake slightly. There will be some precipitation of benzoin in this mixture, but it will settle out, or it may be strained out through cheese cloth.
attribution.notes: Not technically a micellar water (no surfactant), but functions in a similar 'toner / light cleanser' role. The only fresh-ingredient recipe in this initial set.

recipes.name: Tragacanth Cold Cream (Modernized)
recipes.description: Modernized reformulation of Henley's 1907 Tragacanth Cold Cream. Same lightweight tragacanth-jelly profile, but with the historic 10% boric acid reduced to a safe trace, glyconine (egg-yolk glycerite) replaced by lecithin, and a modern broad-spectrum preservative added for water-phase stability.
recipes.notes: Disperse the tragacanth gum into the glycerin first (this prevents clumping). Heat the distilled water to 70°C; add the tragacanth-glycerin mixture slowly with constant stirring (stick blender works well). Once thickened and uniform, add the boric acid and stir until dissolved. Combine almond oil with lecithin in a separate vessel, warm gently to liquify lecithin, then add to the water phase with vigorous mixing — the lecithin emulsifies. Cool to 40°C, then add Geogard Ultra and lavender essential oil. Stir until uniform. pH target: 4.5–5.5 (within Geogard Ultra's effective range). Yields a light, spreadable jelly-cream similar to a modern serum-cream hybrid.

attribution.displayName: Sqrrlbrain Studio (modernized from Henley's 1907)
attribution.author: Sqrrlbrain Studio formulation team
attribution.originalSource: Derived from Henley's Twentieth Century Book of Recipes (1907), 'Cold Cream II' — see pd-002 for verbatim historic source
attribution.notes: Modernization changes: (1) Boric acid reduced from 10% to 0.5% (well below EU 5% adult-cosmetic limit). (2) Glyconine (egg-yolk + glycerin emulsion) replaced by lecithin (soy or sunflower) — stable, vegetarian, easier to source. (3) Geogard Ultra (gluconolactone + sodium benzoate) added for broad-spectrum preservation of the water phase. (4) Process modernized to use stick blender. Verbatim historic source is preserved in pd-002 attribution; this entry is the 'make today' version.

recipes.name: Sparkly Mica Lip Gloss (Inspired by Lipol)
recipes.description: Modern sparkly mica lip gloss derived from Henley's 1907 'Lipol' medicated lip salve. Reformulated for cosmetic (not medicinal) use: camphor and menthol reduced, alkanet root replaced by cosmetic-grade mica for shimmer, bitter almond oil replaced by safer vanilla, candelilla wax added for cleaner texture. The result is a slick, glossy, lightly tingling, sparkly lip product.
recipes.notes: Melt the candelilla wax, petrolatum, and castor oil together in a double boiler until uniform (about 75°C). Remove from heat. Stir in vitamin E. While mixture is still molten but below 60°C, add the menthol, camphor, vanilla, and eucalyptus essential oils. Just before pouring, sift in the mica and stir to disperse evenly (do not over-stir or sparkle settles). Pour into tubes or pots and let set at room temperature. SUBSTITUTION OPTIONS: replace mica with cosmetic-safe glitter for chunkier sparkle (1-3% by weight). For tinted variants, add 0.5-2% iron oxide pigment (red, pink, brown) along with mica. For lower viscosity (more 'gloss', less 'salve'), increase castor oil to 60% and reduce candelilla wax to 8%.

attribution.displayName: Sqrrlbrain Studio (modernized from Henley's 1907)
attribution.author: Sqrrlbrain Studio formulation team
attribution.originalSource: Derived from Henley's Twentieth Century Book of Recipes (1907), 'Lipol' — see pd-003 for verbatim historic source
attribution.notes: Modernization changes: (1) Reframed from medicated lip salve to cosmetic gloss — camphor and menthol reduced from 0.45% each to 0.5% combined-equivalent. (2) Alkanet root (potential sensitizer; finicky infusion) replaced by cosmetic-grade mica for shimmer + color. (3) Bitter almond oil (benzaldehyde safety) replaced by vanilla. (4) Cassia oil (cinnamic aldehyde sensitizer) removed entirely. (5) Castor oil added for shine — standard modern lip-gloss base ingredient. (6) Candelilla wax added (vegan alternative to beeswax; better gloss than pure paraffin). (7) Vitamin E added as antioxidant. This entry fills Ron's 'sparkly mica lip gloss' request directly.

recipes.name: Hand & Body Lotion (Modernized)
recipes.description: Modern emulsion hand-and-body lotion inspired by Henley's 1907 anhydrous Hand Lotion. Reformulated as a proper water-in-oil emulsion with modern emulsifying wax — much lighter feel than the historic anhydrous balm, suitable for daily moisturizing rather than rescue use.
recipes.notes: Heat oil phase (almond oil, emulsifying wax, shea butter, lanolin, cetearyl alcohol) and water phase (distilled water, glycerin) separately to 70°C. Pour water phase into oil phase while stick-blending continuously. Continue blending intermittently as it cools. At 40°C, add Geogard Ultra and fragrance oil; blend briefly. Pour into bottles or jars. SAFETY: original historic version contained 2% boric acid — removed entirely here. Geogard Ultra is the broad-spectrum preservative. Target pH: 5.0–5.5.

attribution.displayName: Sqrrlbrain Studio (modernized from Henley's 1907)
attribution.author: Sqrrlbrain Studio formulation team
attribution.originalSource: Derived from Henley's Twentieth Century Book of Recipes (1907), 'Lotion For The Hands' — see pd-005 for verbatim historic source
attribution.notes: Modernization changes: (1) Converted from anhydrous balm to water-based emulsion (most users today expect 'lotion' to mean pump-bottle texture). (2) Boric acid (2%) removed entirely — modern preservation handled by Geogard Ultra. (3) Shea butter added for skin-feel and to compensate for the dilution from added water. (4) Emulsifying Wax NF + Cetearyl Alcohol create the emulsion structure. (5) Historic glycerin (heavy use in original) preserved at 8% for humectant action.

recipes.name: Rose Cosmetic Jelly (Modernized with Preservative)
recipes.description: Minimal-change modernization of Henley's 1907 Cosmetic Jelly — same tragacanth-in-rosewater base, with a broad-spectrum preservative added so the product is shelf-stable for months rather than days. Optional witch hazel substitution for a more astringent variant.
recipes.notes: Disperse tragacanth gum into the glycerin (prevents clumping). Add to rose hydrosol with vigorous stirring; let stand for 2–4 hours to fully hydrate. Add ethanol and Geogard Ultra; stir until uniform. Bottle in a sterile container. Shelf life: 6+ months at room temp with Geogard Ultra at 1%. VARIANT: replace half the rose hydrosol with witch hazel for a mildly astringent toner-jelly. Apply after bathing or as a hydrating layer under heavier creams.

attribution.author: Sqrrlbrain Studio formulation team
attribution.originalSource: Derived from Henley's Twentieth Century Book of Recipes (1907), 'Cosmetic Jelly' — see pd-006 for verbatim historic source
attribution.notes: Modernization changes: (1) Geogard Ultra (1%) added as broad-spectrum preservative — original was unsafe past a few days of refrigeration. (2) Rose hydrosol substituted for 'rose water' (modern equivalent; cleaner ingredient). (3) Slight reformulation to fit hydrosol density. Otherwise structurally identical to the 1907 recipe.

recipes.name: Cucumber Astringent Toner (Modernized)
recipes.description: Modern toner derived from Henley's 1907 'Astringent Wash for Flabby Skin.' Fresh cucumber juice (spoilage risk) replaced by cucumber hydrosol; cologne replaced by witch hazel; preservative added. Functions as a daily astringent toner for oily or combination skin.
recipes.notes: Combine cucumber hydrosol, witch hazel, elder flower hydrosol, and glycerin in a clean bottle. Add Geogard Ultra and citric acid; shake to dissolve. Add tincture of benzoin LAST and shake vigorously — benzoin may precipitate slightly; this is expected and can be left to settle or strained out. pH target: 4.5–5.5 (verify with strips; adjust citric acid if needed). Shelf life: 6+ months at room temp. Apply with cotton pad after cleansing, or use as a micellar-style oil-cut by dampening pad with toner + a few drops of grapeseed oil before wiping. SAFETY: tincture of benzoin contains ethanol + benzoic acid; total alcohol content of this toner is low (~3%) and skin-safe for most.

attribution.displayName: Sqrrlbrain Studio (modernized from Henley's 1907)
attribution.author: Sqrrlbrain Studio formulation team
attribution.originalSource: Derived from Henley's Twentieth Century Book of Recipes (1907), 'Astringent Wash for Flabby Skin' — see pd-008 for verbatim historic source
attribution.notes: Modernization changes: (1) Fresh cucumber juice → cucumber hydrosol (no spoilage risk, no refrigeration needed). (2) Cologne (perfumed alcohol) → witch hazel (provides astringent action + alcohol content). (3) Geogard Ultra (1%) added — required for any water-based product intended for shelf-stable distribution. (4) Citric acid added for pH targeting (Geogard Ultra is most effective at pH 5 or below). (5) Glycerin added at 3% for humectant softening (counteracts witch-hazel drying).

recipes.name: Hydrating Setting Spray
equipment: fine-mist spray bottle (100 mL+, continuous-mist preferred)
recipes.description: A simple humectant-based cosmetic setting spray. Glycerin acts as the makeup binder; witch hazel adds light astringency for set + oil control; apricot kernel oil contributes a soft glow without heaviness; preservative ensures shelf stability. Designed for normal to dry skin.
recipes.notes: Sanitize the spray bottle with 70% isopropyl alcohol and let it dry. Combine distilled water, witch hazel, and glycerin in the bottle. Add apricot kernel oil and Vitamin E. Add preservative last. Shake vigorously before every use — oil and water will separate (this is expected without an emulsifier). Apply 8–10 inches from face in an X-and-T motion. SKIN-TYPE ADJUSTMENTS: for oily skin, reduce glycerin to 5% and increase witch hazel to 20%; for very dry skin, increase glycerin to 15% and add 1% sodium PCA. PRESERVATION: Liquid Germall Plus at 0.5% gives shelf stability for 6+ months at room temp. Without preservative, refrigerate and discard after 2 weeks.

attribution.displayName: Sqrrlbrain Studio
attribution.author: Sqrrlbrain Studio formulation team
attribution.notes: Standard cosmetic-chemistry humectant-occlusive formulation. Not derived from a specific copyrighted source — uses well-known DIY-cosmetic principles (humectant glycerin + witch hazel astringent + light oil + preservative). Recipe fills the 'setting spray' category for which no PD historic analog exists.

recipes.name: Multichrome Glitter Setting Spray
equipment: fine-mist spray bottle (100 mL+, must be ≥20-micron nozzle to avoid clogging)
recipes.description: A sparkly multichrome setting spray that locks makeup in place while adding a color-shifting glitter finish. PVP K-30 acts as a film-former (the same polymer used in commercial setting sprays and hairsprays), giving the spray a 'set and forget' hold rather than a sticky residue. Use ultra-fine multichrome mica (<20 microns) to avoid nozzle clogging.
recipes.notes:
Sanitize bottle and tools with 70% isopropyl alcohol. STEP 1 — PIGMENT SLURRY: In a small cup, mix the multichrome mica with the glycerin first. Stir until smooth and clump-free — this 'wets' the pigment so it disperses cleanly rather than floating. STEP 2 — POLYMER: Sprinkle PVP K-30 slowly over the surface of the distilled water. Let it sit undisturbed for 5 minutes to hydrate (avoids 'fish-eye' clumps), then stir gently until fully dissolved. STEP 3 — COMBINE: Add the glycerin-pigment slurry, witch hazel, panthenol, and hyaluronic acid to the PVP/water mixture. Stir for 2 minutes until uniform. STEP 4 — PRESERVE: Add Liquid Germall Plus last. Stir briefly. STEP 5 — BOTTLE: Use a funnel to transfer to spray bottle. Shake before each use — mica settles even with film-former.

NOZZLE CRITICAL: Standard setting-spray nozzles clog with mica. Use a fine-mist nozzle rated for cosmetic suspensions, or test the bottle with plain water first.

NOTE ON COLOR SHIFT: Multichrome flakes lay best on a slightly sticky surface — for maximum color-shift visibility, apply over a gel primer or a tacky base. On bare skin, color shift will be subtle.

STORAGE: PVP K-30 is hygroscopic in dry form — keep the powder in a sealed container with a desiccant pack. Finished spray is stable 6+ months at room temp with Liquid Germall Plus.

attribution.displayName: Sqrrlbrain Studio
attribution.author: Sqrrlbrain Studio formulation team
attribution.notes: Uses standard cosmetic-chemistry building blocks: PVP K-30 film former (industry-standard hair-spray polymer), humectant glycerin, witch-hazel astringent, panthenol skin-conditioner, multichrome mica pigment. Not a clone of any specific commercial setting spray — built from publicly-known chemistry principles. PVP K-30 sourcing: small-quantity from Lotioncrafter (gold standard, COA provided) or VedaOils; larger volumes from MakingCosmetics. PVP K-30 is hygroscopic — store sealed with desiccant. For visible color shift, recommend application over a gel primer.

recipes.name: Concentrated Soda Ash Laundry Powder
equipment: large bucket (5 gal+) with airtight lid
cheese grater or food processor for soap
recipes.description: A highly concentrated dry laundry detergent built on sodium carbonate (soda ash) as the primary alkaline cleaner, grated castile bar soap as the plant-based surfactant, citric acid as rinse aid and machine descaler, and fragrance oil for scenting. Intentionally omits sodium bicarbonate — formulated for households with baking-soda sensitivities. One tablespoon per standard load; this batch lasts 5+ years at 7 loads/week.
recipes.notes:
PROPORTIONS: roughly 4:1 soda ash to castile soap by weight, with citric acid at ~10% of the soda-ash amount. SCALE (Ron's actual production batch, May 2026): 25 lbs soda ash + 6.24 lbs grated castile soap (24 × 118g bars) + 2.5 lbs citric acid + 8 oz fragrance oil per 5-gal bucket; total 34 lbs per bucket; lasts ~1000 loads.

INSTRUCTIONS:
1. Grate castile bars on the finest grater side — aim for 'snowflakes,' not chunks, so they dissolve in the wash.
2. Wear a dust mask. In a large bucket, whisk the soda ash and citric acid together (soda ash dust is alkaline and irritating to airways).
3. Drizzle the fragrance oil over the powder mix BEFORE adding the soap flakes. Stir thoroughly to distribute scent evenly.
4. Fold in the grated soap flakes; stir gently — the powder will coat the soap, keeping it free-flowing.
5. Stir again after 24 hours to redistribute any settled oil.
6. Store in airtight 5-gal buckets with gamma-seal lids; citric acid + soda ash are both hygroscopic, and moisture exposure turns the batch into a brick.

USAGE: 1 tablespoon per standard / HE load; 2 tablespoons for heavy-soil loads. Set washer to 'Extra Rinse' for sensitive skin (high pH 11 from pure soda ash).

VARIANTS:
• Standard / bicarbonate-tolerant: Substitute 1/3 of the soda-ash weight with sodium bicarbonate for a milder version (lower pH ~10).
• Heavy-grease: Increase castile soap to 25%, reduce soda ash to ~65%.
• Unscented: Omit fragrance oil; expect a soft soap scent from the castile alone.

ADJACENT USES (with caveats — fragrance oil residue may stain or streak): dishwasher detergent at 1 tsp/load (test in dishwasher first; can over-suds), toilet bowl scrub (2 tbsp + sit 15 min + brush + flush). Do NOT use on glass, food-prep surfaces, or unsealed wood.

SAFETY: High alkalinity (pH 11). Wear gloves when handling concentrated mix. Not safe on silk/wool delicates. Keep away from food-prep surfaces because fragrance oils are not food-grade.

attribution.displayName: Sqrrlbrain Studio
attribution.author: Ron Goodrich + Sqrrlbrain Studio formulation team
attribution.verifiedBy: Ron Goodrich (formulated and produced in actual bulk batch, May 2026)
attribution.notes: Ron produced two 5-gallon buckets of this formulation in May 2026 (50 lb soda ash total) and is using it as his household's laundry detergent. The 'no sodium bicarbonate' constraint exists because Ron's wife is allergic to baking soda — see project_wife_baking_soda_allergy memory. Inspired by Buff City Soap's dry-detergent format (5-ingredient base of soda ash + bicarb + soap + citric acid + fragrance); this recipe diverges by dropping the bicarb entirely and rebalancing for higher alkaline cleaning power. Cost analysis: ~$250 for the bulk batch vs. ~$544 retail-equivalent in 850g containers = ~$294 saved per double-batch, or ~$0.23/load.

recipes.name: Gentle Everyday Micellar Water
recipes.description: A true micellar water with decyl glucoside as the gentle surfactant — micelles trap and lift dirt and oil without rinsing. Balanced for daily use; safe around the eyes. Distinct from the toner-style sd-005 (which has no surfactant); this one actually cleanses.
recipes.notes: Sanitize bottle and tools with 70% isopropyl alcohol. Stir the glycerin and witch hazel into the distilled water until uniform. Add the decyl glucoside SLOWLY — fast stirring will create foam that's hard to settle. Add Liquid Germall Plus last; stir gently. Bottle. pH target: 5.0–5.5 (verify with strips; if too alkaline, add a single drop of dilute citric acid solution and re-test). Apply to a cotton pad and wipe over face — no rinsing required. Shelf life: 6+ months at room temp with Liquid Germall Plus. NO PRESERVATIVE VARIANT: skip Germall Plus, refrigerate, use within 3-5 days; make tiny batches.

attribution.displayName: Sqrrlbrain Studio
attribution.author: Sqrrlbrain Studio formulation team
attribution.notes: Standard cosmetic-chemistry micellar-water formulation using decyl glucoside as the mild surfactant (glucose-derived, gentle on eyes, sulfate-free). 5% decyl glucoside is at the high end of typical use (2-10%); reduce to 3-4% for very sensitive skin. Decyl glucoside has a natural pH of ~11-12, so citric-acid pH adjustment is essential. Decyl glucoside sourcing: Lotioncrafter, MakingCosmetics, WSP. Crucible's true micellar entry — pd-008 and sd-005 are toner-style, not surfactant micellar.

recipes.name: Deep Clean Micellar Water (Oil-Solubilized)
recipes.description: A heavier-duty micellar water that uses polysorbate 20 to solubilize a small amount of apricot kernel oil into the water phase. The micelles + oil combination cleans long-wear and waterproof makeup without leaving a greasy residue. Heavier feel than sb-004 (Gentle); same no-rinse application.
recipes.notes:
STEP 1 — SOLUBILIZE OIL: In a small mixing cup, combine the apricot kernel oil with the polysorbate 20. Stir vigorously until uniform — this 'pre-emulsifies' the oil so it disperses in water rather than separating. STEP 2 — WATER PHASE: In your sanitized bottle, combine distilled water, rose water (or aloe juice), and glycerin. STEP 3 — COMBINE: Pour the polysorbate-oil mixture into the water phase slowly with stirring. The water should remain clear or very lightly hazy — if it separates into oil droplets, the polysorbate ratio is too low; add more polysorbate 20 (try 1% increments). STEP 4 — PRESERVE + pH: Add Liquid Germall Plus and citric acid; stir until dissolved. Target pH 4.5–5.5.

USAGE: Apply generously to a cotton pad; sweep over face, eyes, lips. No rinsing required. Will remove waterproof mascara and long-wear foundation that sb-004 (Gentle) cannot handle. Skin will feel softer (less stripped) than alcohol-based makeup removers because of the apricot oil + glycerin.

VARIANTS: Replace apricot kernel oil with hemp seed oil (slightly heavier feel, omega-3 boost) or fractionated coconut oil (lighter feel, longer shelf life).

attribution.displayName: Sqrrlbrain Studio
attribution.author: Sqrrlbrain Studio formulation team
attribution.notes: Solubilized oil-in-water formulation using polysorbate 20 as the solubilizer. Polysorbate 20 has an HLB of 16.7, which is appropriate for 'wetting' light oils into water-based products. The 5:3 polysorbate-to-oil ratio is conservative; if the product looks cloudy or separates, increase polysorbate 20 by 1% increments until clear. Apricot kernel oil is in Ron's existing 706-library inventory (private library), so swap-friendly with hemp seed oil or other light carriers. This sits between sb-004 (gentle, water-only) and a full oil cleanser like pd-001 (heavy, balm-like). For waterproof makeup, this is the right answer.

recipes.name: Whipped Hemp & Apricot Body Butter
equipment: stand mixer or hand mixer (whisk attachment)
recipes.description: A whipped body butter with shea base, apricot kernel oil as the main carrier, hemp seed oil for the antioxidant + omega profile, corn starch to cut the greasy feel and give a silky matte finish, and a 2% fragrance load to overcome the earthy hemp base notes. Whipping doubles the volume — a 198 g batch fluffs to fill a 300 mL container.
recipes.notes:
BATCH SIZE: Calculate by target container, not target volume. Whipping incorporates air and roughly doubles volume. Ron's 300 mL container holds 198 g of whipped body butter (122 g empty container; 320 g full).

INSTRUCTIONS:
1. Gently melt the shea butter in a double boiler or microwave (low heat — shea grains can form if overheated then cooled too fast).
2. Once melted, remove from heat. Stir in the apricot kernel oil and hemp seed oil.
3. Whisk in the corn starch until fully dispersed (no clumps).
4. Cool the mixture in the fridge until it begins to solidify around the edges but is still soft in the center (typically 15-30 minutes).
5. Whip with stand mixer or hand mixer for 3-5 minutes on medium-high until light and fluffy. The mixture will lighten in color and approximately double in volume.
6. Add the fragrance oil at the end of whipping; mix just enough to incorporate (over-mixing after fragrance addition can deflate the whip).
7. Scoop into containers immediately while soft enough to spread; allow to set at room temperature.

VARIANTS:
• Different oils: swap apricot kernel for jojoba, sweet almond, or sunflower (any light carrier oil at the same percentage works).
• Heavier feel: increase shea butter percentage to 60% and reduce corn starch to 10%.
• Lighter feel: increase apricot to 27% and reduce shea to 50%.
• Unscented: omit fragrance, redistribute to corn starch.

SAFETY:
• 2% fragrance is the safe upper limit for leave-on body products. Going higher risks skin sensitization.
• Different essential oils have different max dermal-usage rates. Lavender, vanilla, most florals are fine at 2%. Cinnamon bark, oregano, clove, and citrus oils have STRICTER limits — verify before substituting.
• No water phase = no preservative required. Shelf life is 6-12 months at room temp (limited by oil oxidation, not microbial growth).

attribution.displayName: Sqrrlbrain Studio — Ron Goodrich
attribution.author: Ron Goodrich (formulator)
attribution.verifiedBy: Ron Goodrich (locked as personal go-to formula 2026-05-11; multiple batches produced)
attribution.notes: Ron's locked-in personal body butter recipe, finalized through iteration on 2026-05-11. Started from a generic shea + sunflower + Vitamin E base, evolved through swaps: sunflower → 20% hemp + 80% apricot kernel; Vitamin E dropped to make room for higher fragrance load; fragrance bumped from 0.5% to 2% (max safe for leave-on). The 15% corn starch is the texture differentiator — gives a silky, matte finish instead of the typical greasy shea feel. This is the body butter Ron uses personally and may eventually commercialize as a Sqrrlbrain product.

recipes.name: Castor & Almond Cold Cream
recipes.description: A light cold cream using castor oil as the main carrier with sweet almond oil and white wax. No spermaceti, no lard — one of the cleanest historic cold cream variants in Henley's. Castor oil gives slight slip and gloss.
recipes.notes: Melt the wax in a double boiler at moderate heat. Add the castor oil and almond oil; stir until uniform. Remove from heat and let cool slightly before adding essential oils (preserves volatile top notes). Pour into containers while still pourable. Anhydrous — no preservative required.

attribution.displayName: Henley's Twentieth Century Book of Recipes, Formulas and Processes (1907 / 1914 ed.)
attribution.author: Gardner D. Hiscox (ed.)
attribution.originalRecipe: VI.— Castor oil 500 parts; White wax 100 parts; Almond oil 150 parts. Melt at moderate heat and scent with Geranium oil 6 parts; Lemon oil 5 parts; Bergamot oil 10 parts.
attribution.notes: Direct percentage conversion from parts. One of the few historic cold creams with no spermaceti, no lard, no animal-derived ingredients — modern-makers can produce as-is.

recipes.name: Honey & Almond Cleansing Cream
recipes.description: A rich cleansing cream combining honey's humectant + antimicrobial properties with castile soap and sweet almond oil. Carmine adds a soft rose tint. Closer to a modern hydrating cleansing balm than a typical cold cream.
recipes.notes: Mix honey and powdered castile soap in a mortar until smooth. Add KOH solution slowly to produce a cream consistency. Combine bitter almond, bergamot, and clove oils with Peru balsam and sweet almond oil; add to the honey-soap cream and stir vigorously until uniform. Optional: add carmine solution for a rose tint. SAFETY: KOH is caustic; wear gloves. Bitter almond oil should be verified benzaldehyde-free.

attribution.displayName: Henley's Twentieth Century Book of Recipes, Formulas and Processes (1907 / 1914 ed.)
attribution.author: Gardner D. Hiscox (ed.)
attribution.originalRecipe: XI.— Honey 2 av. ounces; Castile soap, white powder 1 av. ounce; Oil sweet almonds 26 fluidounces; Oil bitter almonds 1 fluidrachm; Oil bergamot 1/2 fluidrachm; Oil cloves 15 drops; Peru balsam 1 fluidrachm; Liquor potassa, Solution carmine, of each sufficient.
attribution.notes: Saponified honey-soap base — the KOH partially saponifies free fatty acids producing a self-emulsifying cream. Functionally a cleansing balm; rinse off with warm water.

recipes.name: Simple Glycerin Cream
recipes.description: A three-ingredient base cream — sweet almond oil, white wax, glycerin. As minimal as a real cream can get. Functions as both an emollient and a base for custom essential oil scenting.
recipes.notes: Melt the wax and oil together on a water bath. Add glycerin and stir until uniform. Remove from heat; as the mass cools, add essential oil(s) of choice. Pour into containers while still warm. Glycerin is hygroscopic but not free water — no preservative strictly required; add a drop of Vitamin E to delay oxidation.

attribution.displayName: Henley's Twentieth Century Book of Recipes, Formulas and Processes (1907 / 1914 ed.)
attribution.author: Gardner D. Hiscox (ed.)
attribution.originalRecipe: I.— Oil of sweet almonds 100 parts; White wax 13 parts; Glycerine, pure 25 parts. Add a sufficient quantity of any suitable perfume. Melt, on the water bath, the oil, wax, and glycerine together, remove and as the mass cools down add the perfume in sufficient quantity to make a creamy mass.
attribution.notes: Simplest viable cold-cream-style recipe in the chapter. Excellent starting base for modification.

recipes.name: Lanolin & Peach Kernel Cream
recipes.description: A rich anhydrous-leaning lanolin cream with peach kernel oil (light, skin-similar to apricot kernel). Perfumed with ionone (violet) or synthetic ylang-ylang.
recipes.notes: Melt lanolin in a double boiler. Add peach kernel oil; stir until uniform. Transfer to a mortar and slowly incorporate water with continuous stirring — lanolin holds water well (~2:1 capacity). When cooled, add perfume (about 15 drops ionone or 20 drops ylang-ylang per 100g batch). SUBSTITUTION: peach kernel ↔ apricot kernel (very similar fatty acid profile).

attribution.displayName: Henley's Twentieth Century Book of Recipes, Formulas and Processes (1907 / 1914 ed.)
attribution.author: Gardner D. Hiscox (ed.)
attribution.originalRecipe: I.— Anhydrous lanolin 650 parts; Peach-kernel oil 200 parts; Water 150 parts. Perfume with about 15 drops of ionone or 20 drops of synthetic ylang-ylang.
attribution.notes: Lanolin's intrinsic water-holding means the 15% water phase is bound, not free. Add Geogard Ultra at 0.5% for batches >3 months.

recipes.name: Lanolin Face Cream (Light Formula)
recipes.description: A lighter lanolin cream — adds paraffin and orange-flower water (aqua naphae) for floral notes, with boric acid and borax for mild antimicrobial action.
recipes.notes: Melt lanolin and paraffin together. Add olive oil. Separately dissolve boric acid and borax in the warm water + orange-flower water + glycerin. Combine slowly with constant stirring. Add essential oils below 40°C. SAFETY: boric acid at 3.8% is near EU adult limit (5%); reduce to 1-2% for sensitive skin. Modern alternative: replace borax/boric with Geogard Ultra at 0.75%.

attribution.displayName: Henley's Twentieth Century Book of Recipes, Formulas and Processes (1907 / 1914 ed.)
attribution.author: Gardner D. Hiscox (ed.)
attribution.originalRecipe: II.— Lanolin 40 parts; Olive oil 15 parts; Paraffine ointment 10 parts; Aqua naphæ 10 parts; Distilled water 15 parts; Glycerine 5 parts; Boric acid 4 parts; Borax 4 parts; Geranium oil, sufficient. Extract, triple, of ylang-ylang, quantity sufficient.
attribution.notes: More complete than the simpler Lanolin Cream I (pd-012) — adds water phase, humectant, and borax/boric antimicrobial pair. Closer to true emulsion.

recipes.name: Witch Hazel & Quince Seed Cream
recipes.description: A water-light cream built on witch-hazel extract with quince-seed mucilage as thickener and glycerin. Quince seed releases a clear mucilage when soaked — historic equivalent of xanthan gum.
recipes.notes: Macerate quince seeds in hot water for 2-3 hours until mucilage gels. Strain through cheesecloth. Combine with glycerin and witch hazel; stir until uniform. Dissolve boric acid. Let stand 2 days, stirring occasionally. Strain and add rose and violet extracts. SAFETY: reduce boric acid to 0.5-1% for sensitive skin. Quince seed available from herb suppliers as Cydonia oblonga.

attribution.displayName: Henley's Twentieth Century Book of Recipes, Formulas and Processes (1907 / 1914 ed.)
attribution.author: Gardner D. Hiscox (ed.)
attribution.originalRecipe: II.— Quince seed 4 ounces; Hot water 16 ounces; Glycerine 32 ounces; Witch-hazel water 128 ounces; Boric acid 6 ounces; Rose extract 2 ounces; Violet extract 1 ounce.
attribution.notes: Quince seed mucilage — a fascinating historic thickener. Cleaner-feeling than xanthan or carbomer.

recipes.name: Grease-Free Quince Seed Face Gel
recipes.description: A grease-free hydrating face gel — water + quince-seed mucilage + glycerin + alcohol. Historic version of a modern lightweight hydrating gel-serum. Rose-perfumed; sets to a non-greasy film on skin.
recipes.notes: Boil half the water and macerate quince seed for 2.5 hours; strain off mucilage. In remaining hot water, dissolve borax and boric acid; add glycerin and rose (predissolved in alcohol). Slowly add quince mucilage to the alcoholic-aqueous solution under constant stirring for 5 minutes after the last addition. Bottle. Add Geogard Ultra at 0.75% for shelf-stable production.

attribution.displayName: Henley's Twentieth Century Book of Recipes, Formulas and Processes (1907 / 1914 ed.)
attribution.author: Gardner D. Hiscox (ed.)
attribution.originalRecipe: Quince seed 10 parts; Boiling water 1,000 parts; Borax 5 parts; Boric acid 5 parts; Glycerine 100 parts; Alcohol, 94 per cent 125 parts; Attar of rose, quantity sufficient to perfume.
attribution.notes: Essentially a clear hydrating serum. Quince mucilage gives body without an oil phase.

recipes.name: Glycerin Toilet Milk
recipes.description: A toilet milk — pre-water-emulsion hydrating product. Glycerin + starch base creates a milky-white finish; tincture of benzoin adds resinous antimicrobial action and balsamic scent.
recipes.notes: Combine half the starch with glycerin in a steam bath, stirring until it forms a jelly-like mass. Remove from heat; stir in remaining starch. Add water and tincture of benzoin; stir until homogeneous. Add Geogard Ultra at 0.75% for retail-grade shelf stability.

attribution.displayName: Henley's Twentieth Century Book of Recipes, Formulas and Processes (1907 / 1914 ed.)
attribution.author: Gardner D. Hiscox (ed.)
attribution.originalRecipe: Glycerine 1,150 parts; Starch, powdered 160 parts; Distilled water 400 parts; Tincture of benzoin 20 parts.
attribution.notes: Milk aesthetic from starch suspended in glycerin. Modern alternative starches: cornstarch or arrowroot.

recipes.name: Lanolin Toilet Milk
recipes.description: A lanolin-based toilet milk emulsified with white castile soap. Softer feel than the all-glycerin pd-016 because of lanolin emollience. Tincture of benzoin adds resinous antimicrobial action.
recipes.notes: Dissolve soap in half the warm water. Separately, mix lanolin with the other half of warm water. Combine; stir until uniform. Add tincture of benzoin last. SUBSTITUTION: 90 grains powdered borax can replace tincture of benzoin per the source. Needs Geogard Ultra 0.75% for retail-grade shelf life.

attribution.displayName: Henley's Twentieth Century Book of Recipes, Formulas and Processes (1907 / 1914 ed.)
attribution.author: Gardner D. Hiscox (ed.)
attribution.originalSource: Henley's — COSMETICS, 'Toilet Milks — Lanolin Toilet Milk'
attribution.originalRecipe: White castile soap, powdered 22 grains; Lanolin 1 ounce; Tincture benzoin 12 drachms; Water, enough.
attribution.notes: Lanolin + castile soap creates a self-emulsifying milky cleanser. Functionally a modern milky cleansing lotion.

recipes.name: Boric Acid Gelatin Jelly
recipes.description: A simple gelatin-based jelly with glycerin and boric acid — historic substitute for cucumber cream. Sets to a clear hydrating gel; can be used as a mask or layered under heavier creams.
recipes.notes: Sprinkle gelatin over half the hot water; bloom 5 minutes. Add rest of hot water; stir to dissolve. Stir in glycerin and boric acid. Strain into containers; refrigerate to set. SUBSTITUTION: agar agar (1-2%) for vegan version. Reduce boric acid to 0.5-1% for sensitive skin.

attribution.displayName: Henley's Twentieth Century Book of Recipes, Formulas and Processes (1907 / 1914 ed.)
attribution.author: Gardner D. Hiscox (ed.)
attribution.originalRecipe: IV.—This is offered as a substitute for cucumber cream for toilet uses. Melt 15 parts, by weight, of gelatin in hot water containing 15 parts, by weight, of boracic acid as well as 150 parts, by weight, of glycerine; the total amount of water used should not exceed 300 parts, by weight.
attribution.notes: Functions like a modern collagen-jelly mask — minimal ingredients, hydrating, cooling.

recipes.name: Hair-Curling & Setting Liquid
recipes.description: Historic ancestor of modern hair setting spray — water + alcohol + tincture of benzoin + perfume. Henley's notes it can't make straight hair curly, but extends and protects existing curls against humidity.
recipes.notes: Combine all ingredients in a spray bottle and shake until uniform. Apply to damp hair before styling, or mist over set curls to lock in. The benzoin adds resin film-former action; if substituting borax (2 parts per 100 — Henley's variant I), you get matte finish without film. High alcohol content is self-preserving.

attribution.displayName: Henley's Twentieth Century Book of Recipes, Formulas and Processes (1907 / 1914 ed.)
attribution.author: Gardner D. Hiscox (ed.)
attribution.originalRecipe: II — Water 80; Spirit of wine 20; Tincture of benzoin 3; Perfume ad. lib. (Variant I uses Borax 2 parts in place of the benzoin.)
attribution.notes: Genuine historic hair-setting analog. Source explicitly states it cannot make straight hair curly; it extends and protects existing curls. Effectively a 1907 setting spray for hair.

recipes.name: Rosemary Hair Water
recipes.description: A clear rosemary-infused hair tonic — magnesia acts as a filter aid to clarify rosemary oil into the water phase. Historic scalp treatment; rosemary is known for circulation-stimulating action.
recipes.notes: Mix rosemary oil with spirit of wine in a mortar. Add magnesia and rub until uniform — magnesia binds the volatile oil into fine suspension. Slowly add distilled water with continuous stirring. Filter through fine cloth or coffee filter — magnesia carries the rosemary oil into the water phase, producing a clear, perfumed tonic. Apply to scalp; massage in. Add Geogard Ultra at 0.75% for batches over 1 week.

attribution.displayName: Henley's Twentieth Century Book of Recipes, Formulas and Processes (1907 / 1914 ed.)
attribution.author: Gardner D. Hiscox (ed.)
attribution.originalRecipe: IV.— Rosemary oil 1.5 parts; Rectified spirit of wine 7 parts; Magnesia 7 parts; Distilled water 1,000 parts.
attribution.notes: Magnesia + alcohol pre-trituration is an elegant historic technique for getting essential oils evenly distributed in water — modern alternative is polysorbate 20.

recipes.name: Bay Rum (Traditional Aftershave)
recipes.description: Classic Bay Rum aftershave/toilet water — oil of bay (Pimenta racemosa), alcohol, water. The historic gentleman's aftershave. Filter through magnesia for clarity.
recipes.notes: Combine oil of bay, alcohol, and water in a jar. Add a small amount of magnesia (magnesium oxide); shake thoroughly. Filter through coffee filter or paper — the magnesia carries any undissolved oil out, leaving a clear amber liquid. Bottle. Apply after shaving. High alcohol content is self-preserving.

attribution.displayName: Henley's Twentieth Century Book of Recipes, Formulas and Processes (1907 / 1914 ed.)
attribution.author: Gardner D. Hiscox (ed.)
attribution.originalRecipe: I.— Oil of bay 1 drachm; Alcohol 18 ounces; Water 18 ounces. Mix and filter through magnesia.
attribution.notes: Simplest variant. Henley's Variant II adds Jamaica rum (2 parts) + bay-leaf otto + extra alcohol — richer/spicier; substitute dark rum if you want the spirit-warmth note.

recipes.name: Birch-Bud Toilet Water
recipes.description: An herbal toilet water — birch-bud essential oil + spring flower essence + soft soap + glycerin. Chlorophyll tints it green. A unique woodsy/floral scent profile distinct from typical rose/lavender colognes.
recipes.notes: Mix water with an equal volume of spirit; dissolve the soap in this mixture. Mix the birch bud oil and flower essence with the remaining spirit. Combine the two; add chlorophyll for tint. Agitate well; let stand 8 days; filter. To use, dilute 1:1 with water before applying as a refreshing splash. Long maceration (8 days) develops the scent.

attribution.displayName: Henley's Twentieth Century Book of Recipes, Formulas and Processes (1907 / 1914 ed.)
attribution.author: Gardner D. Hiscox (ed.)
attribution.originalRecipe: Alcohol (96 per cent), 350 parts; water, 70 parts; soft soap, 20 parts; glycerine, 15 parts; essential oil of birch buds, 5 parts; essence of spring flowers, 10 parts; chlorophyll, quantity sufficient to tint.
attribution.notes: Soap + glycerin presence gives this a slightly emollient finish — sits between a toilet water and a body splash. Unique scent profile.

recipes.name: Carmelite Balm Water
recipes.description: Carmelite Balm Water — a classical apothecary toilet water dating back to the 14th-century Carmelite Order. Complex spice + citrus + herb blend in alcohol. Historic remedy for headaches and nervous tension; modern use as toilet water/cologne.
recipes.notes: Combine all essential oils in the alcohol; shake well; let stand 1-2 weeks to mature before use. Apply as a cologne. SAFETY: cinnamon and clove oils at this concentration are at typical-use rates for skin-contact products, but verify against current IFRA limits if commercializing.

attribution.displayName: Henley's Twentieth Century Book of Recipes, Formulas and Processes (1907 / 1914 ed.)
attribution.author: Gardner D. Hiscox (ed.)
attribution.originalRecipe: Melissa oil 30 minims; Sweet marjoram oil 3 minims; Cinnamon oil 10 minims; Angelica oil 3 minims; Citron oil 30 minims; Clove oil 15 minims; Coriander oil 5 minims; Nutmeg oil 5 minims; Alcohol (90 per cent) 10 fluidounces.
attribution.notes: Traditional 'Eau de Mélisse des Carmes' formulation. Historic medicinal use — apply to temples for headaches. Modern use: distinctive complex spice-citrus cologne.

recipes.name: Lilac Toilet Water
recipes.description: A floral lilac-scented toilet water using terpineol (lilac-like aroma compound), heliotropin (vanilla-cherry note), bergamot, and neroli. Brighter, lighter than the spice-heavy Carmelite Balm Water (pd-023).
recipes.notes: Combine terpineol, bergamot oil, heliotropin, and neroli in the alcohol. Shake until heliotropin dissolves. Slowly add distilled water with stirring — solution may go slightly cloudy initially, will clarify on standing. Let stand 2-3 days; filter if needed. Bottle. SOURCING: terpineol and heliotropin available from cosmetic fragrance suppliers (MakingCosmetics, Lotioncrafter).

attribution.displayName: Henley's Twentieth Century Book of Recipes, Formulas and Processes (1907 / 1914 ed.)
attribution.author: Gardner D. Hiscox (ed.)
attribution.originalRecipe: Terpineol 2 drachms; Heliotropin 8 grains; Bergamot oil 1 drachm; Neroli oil 8 minims; Alcohol 12 ounces; Water 4 ounces.
attribution.notes: Terpineol is a naturally-occurring monoterpene also synthesized commercially — gives lilac/lily-of-the-valley character. Heliotropin (piperonal) is the warm cherry-vanilla compound from heliotrope and sassafras.

recipes.name: Orange Flower Toilet Water
recipes.description: A clear orange-flower toilet water using magnesium carbonate as a filter aid to bring the volatile essence into clear water. Refreshing daily splash; classic Mediterranean fragrance.
recipes.notes: Triturate the orange flower essence with the magnesium carbonate in a mortar — the magnesia binds the essential oils into a fine suspension. Slowly add distilled water with continuous stirring. Filter through fine cloth or coffee filter — magnesia carries the orange oil into the water phase, producing a clear scented water. CLARIFYING TIP: if the water remains turbid, shake with washed sand (boiled in hydrochloric acid then rinsed) and filter again. SHELF LIFE: add Geogard Ultra at 0.75% for any batch over 1 week.

attribution.displayName: Henley's Twentieth Century Book of Recipes, Formulas and Processes (1907 / 1914 ed.)
attribution.author: Gardner D. Hiscox (ed.)
attribution.originalRecipe: Orange flower essence 8 ounces; Magnesium carbonate 1 ounce; Water 8 pints. Triturate the essence with the magnesium carbonate, add the water, and filter.
attribution.notes: Same technique as pd-020 (Rosemary Hair Water) — magnesium carbonate as filter aid for essential oils. Reusable approach for any clear scented water you want to make.

recipes.name: Eau de Botot Toilet Water
recipes.description: Eau de Botot — historic French toilet water dating to 1755, originally a court fragrance. Anise + clove + cinnamon + cochineal-red tint in a rose-water-and-spirit base. Distinctive spicy-licorice character.
recipes.notes: Crush the aniseed, clove, and cinnamon. Combine all ingredients in an amber glass jar. Digest (macerate) for 8 days, shaking daily. Strain through fine cloth, then filter. Bottle. SUBSTITUTION: cochineal is insect-derived (carmine source) — for a vegan version, substitute beetroot powder or a CC-licensed plant-derived red colorant. The original 1755 court formulation used cochineal for the signature ruby tint.

attribution.displayName: Henley's Twentieth Century Book of Recipes, Formulas and Processes (1907 / 1914 ed.)
attribution.author: Gardner D. Hiscox (ed.)
attribution.originalRecipe: Aniseed 80 parts; Clover 20 parts; Cinnamon cassia 20 parts; Cochineal 5 parts; Refined spirit 800 parts; Rose water 200 parts. Digest for 8 days...
attribution.notes: Original Eau de Botot was a mouthwash (Edme-François Julien Botot, dentist to Louis XV, 1755). The historic toilet-water version (Henley's recipe) is essentially the same formula at lower dilution. Note Henley's typo 'Clover' (probably 'Clove').

recipes.name: Shaving Paste (Tragacanth Paraffin Emulsion)
recipes.description: A shaving paste built on a paraffin wax emulsion with tragacanth gum as the emulsifier. Lavender-scented. Forms a thin mechanical layer that fills skin depressions and supports the razor — distinct from lather-based shaving soaps.
recipes.notes: Make a tragacanth mucilage with a small portion of the warm water; set aside. Melt the paraffin and stearic acid (or lard) in a double boiler. Add the tragacanth mucilage to the melted wax with vigorous stirring; the emulsion forms as you blend. Add the remaining warm water in stages. When cooled, add alcohol and lavender oil. Final consistency: thick white cream. APPLY a small quantity to the area before shaving; as water evaporates, paraffin particles form a mechanical support layer. About 1 oz lasts 6 shaves.

attribution.displayName: Henley's Twentieth Century Book of Recipes, Formulas and Processes (1907 / 1914 ed.)
attribution.author: Gardner D. Hiscox (ed.)
attribution.originalRecipe: An emulsion of paraffine wax, melting at 131° F., should be used. This is prepared with 25 per cent of wax and 2 per cent of tragacanth, the wax being melted and mixed with the tragacanth previously made into a mucilage with some of the water. The addition of a little stearine or lard renders the emulsification of the wax easier, while about 10 per cent of alcohol makes the preparation more agreeable to use. The fatty odor of the preparation may be covered by the addition of 1/2 to 1 per cent of lavender oil.
attribution.notes: Unique non-lather shaving cream — most shaving products are saponified (soap-based foam). This is mechanical: paraffin particles fill skin pits to support the razor. Vegan version: use vegetable stearic acid instead of lard.

recipes.name: Wintergreen Tooth Powder
recipes.description: Classic saponaceous white tooth powder — precipitated chalk base + castile soap + Florentine orris root for flavor-masking + sugar + oil of wintergreen. Henley's calls it the most popular formula of the era.
recipes.notes: All solid ingredients should be in the finest possible powder and well dried. Triturate the wintergreen oil with part of the chalk first, then mix with the balance of the chalk. Sift each ingredient separately through a #80 or finer sieve; mix all together; sift the mixture 5-6 more times. The finer the sieve and more sifting, the lighter and finer the powder. Cost in 1907: ~15 cents/pound.

attribution.displayName: Henley's Twentieth Century Book of Recipes, Formulas and Processes (1907 / 1914 ed.)
attribution.author: Gardner D. Hiscox (ed.)
attribution.originalRecipe: I.— Precipitated chalk 1 pound; White castile soap 1 ounce; Florentine orris 2 ounces; Sugar 1 ounce; Oil of wintergreen 1/4 ounce.
attribution.notes: Henley's note: avoid pumice, charcoal, cuttlebone — too abrasive. Precipitated chalk is gentle. SAFETY: modern dental advice is to use fluoride toothpastes for cavity prevention; this powder is for stain/plaque mechanical removal only.

recipes.name: Rose Pink Tooth Powder
recipes.description: A rose-flavored pink tooth powder — same chalk base as pd-028 with castile soap and orris, tinted pink with carmine, rose-scented. Caswell-and-Hazard / Hudnut / McMahan style popular in early-1900s New York.
recipes.notes: Process is identical to the wintergreen tooth powder (pd-028) — finest possible powder, triturate rose oil and carmine with part of the chalk, mix with the balance, sift multiple times. The carmine tints the powder a soft pink. SUBSTITUTION: for vegan, replace carmine with beetroot powder or pink kaolin clay (also adds gentle abrasion).

attribution.displayName: Henley's Twentieth Century Book of Recipes, Formulas and Processes (1907 / 1914 ed.)
attribution.author: Gardner D. Hiscox (ed.)
attribution.originalRecipe: II.— Precipitated chalk 1 pound; Florentine orris 2 ounces; Sugar 1 1/2 ounces; White castile soap 1 ounce; No. 40 carmine 15 grains.
attribution.notes: Original was made both with and without soap. Pink color from carmine; rose flavor optional but classic for this style.

recipes.name: Quillaia & Lanolin Hair Wash
recipes.description: A creamy plant-based shampoo using quillaia bark (soapbark — natural saponin source) plus lanolin for conditioning. Forms a thin milky liquid with a cream-like fat layer on top that's redistributed by shaking.
recipes.notes: Extract the quillaia bark in part of the water for several days (this releases the natural saponins). Mix the resulting percolate with the alcohol and filter after settling. Warm the filtrate to the temperature at which wool grease becomes liquid (~40°C); blend in the lanolin with agitation. Top off with water containing 15% spirit of wine to make a 300-part total. SHELF LIFE: needs preservative — add Geogard Ultra 0.75% for retail-grade. Shake before use; the cream layer on top is normal.

attribution.displayName: Henley's Twentieth Century Book of Recipes, Formulas and Processes (1907 / 1914 ed.)
attribution.author: Gardner D. Hiscox (ed.)
attribution.originalRecipe: Extract 4 parts quillaia bark with 36 parts water for several days, mix the percolate with 4 parts alcohol, and filter after having settled. Agitate 40 parts of the filtrate at a temperature at which wool grease becomes liquid, with 12 parts anhydrous lanolin, and fill up with water to which 15 per cent spirit of wine has been added, to 300 parts.
attribution.notes: Quillaia (Quillaja saponaria, soapbark tree) is the historic plant-based shampoo source — saponins create a natural lather. Still used in modern shampoos and as a foaming agent in root beer.

recipes.name: Olive Oil Brilliantine
recipes.description: Simple liquid hair dressing — olive oil, glycerin, alcohol. Shake before use (it separates). Adds shine and a soft conditioning effect without being heavy.
recipes.notes: Combine all in a bottle; shake before each use. The alcohol and glycerin keep some of the oil suspended; full emulsion requires polysorbate 20 (~5%) for a non-separating modern version. Apply sparingly to dry or damp hair.

attribution.displayName: Henley's Twentieth Century Book of Recipes, Formulas and Processes (1907 / 1914 ed.)
attribution.author: Gardner D. Hiscox (ed.)
attribution.originalRecipe: I.— Olive oil, 4 parts; glycerine, 3 parts; alcohol, 3 parts; scent as desired. Shake before use.
attribution.notes: The simplest hair dressing in the book. Substitute jojoba or argan oil for a more modern feel.

recipes.name: Yellow Castor Brilliantine
recipes.description: Castor oil + alcohol hair brilliantine tinted yellow with saffron. Heavier shine than the olive oil version (pd-031) thanks to castor's viscosity. Saffron gives a warm gold tint.
recipes.notes: Steep saffron threads in the alcohol for 24 hours to extract the yellow color; strain. Mix the colored alcohol with castor oil and essential oil. Bottle. SUBSTITUTION: saffron is expensive — substitute turmeric (much cheaper) or annatto for similar gold tint. APPLY a small amount only; castor oil is sticky in excess.

attribution.displayName: Henley's Twentieth Century Book of Recipes, Formulas and Processes (1907 / 1914 ed.)
attribution.author: Gardner D. Hiscox (ed.)
attribution.originalRecipe: II.— Castor oil, 1 part; alcohol, 2 parts; saffron to dye yellow. Scent as desired.
attribution.notes: Castor oil is a classic hair-shine ingredient still used in modern hair-growth oils.

recipes.name: Sesame Hair Oil (Lavender-Bergamot)
recipes.description: Simple plant-based hair oil — sesame or sunflower oil scented with lavender + bergamot + geranium. Inexpensive, multi-purpose; doubles as a body oil or massage oil.
recipes.notes: Combine all in a bottle; shake. Apply sparingly. VARIANT (Henley's II): replace bergamot with lemon oil (20 parts) + rosemary oil (5 parts) for a brighter citrus-herbaceous scent profile. NOTE: bergamot is photosensitizing in non-FCF form — use bergamot FCF (furanocoumarin-free) if applying before sun exposure.

attribution.displayName: Henley's Twentieth Century Book of Recipes, Formulas and Processes (1907 / 1914 ed.)
attribution.author: Gardner D. Hiscox (ed.)
attribution.originalSource: Henley's — HAIR PREPARATIONS, 'A Cheap Hair Oil I'
attribution.originalRecipe: I.— Sesame oil or sunflower oil, 1,000 parts; lavender oil, 15 parts; bergamot oil, 10 parts; and geranium oil, 5 parts.
attribution.notes: Henley's titled this 'A Cheap Hair Oil' — quality wasn't the goal, accessibility was. Still works as a daily hair-and-body oil.

recipes.name: Lavender Bath Powder (Non-Effervescent)
recipes.description: A non-effervescent bath powder — equal parts powdered soap and powdered borax, perfumed with essential oils. Sprinkled into bathwater for a softening, mildly cleansing soak. No fizz (distinct from pd-004 effervescent tablets).
recipes.notes: Sift the powdered soap and powdered borax together to remove clumps. Drizzle lavender oil over the powder and stir to distribute. Store in airtight container. USAGE: 2-3 tablespoons per bath. SCENT VARIANTS: replace lavender with rose geranium + lavender (1:6 by weight) for a rose-floral scent; or use a full cologne blend (lavender 4 + rosemary 4 + bergamot 8 + lemon 16 + clove 4) for a richer profile.

attribution.displayName: Henley's Twentieth Century Book of Recipes, Formulas and Processes (1907 / 1914 ed.)
attribution.author: Gardner D. Hiscox (ed.)
attribution.originalSource: Henley's — BATH TABLETS, EFFERVESCENT (closing paragraph: non-effervescent variant)
attribution.originalRecipe: These mixtures may also be used in the preparation of a bath powder (non-effervescent) made by mixing equal parts of powdered soap and powdered borax.
attribution.notes: Companion to pd-004 (effervescent bath tablets). The non-fizzing version is more about water-softening and gentle cleansing than the sensory experience of carbonation.

recipes.name: Cologne Bath Powder (Premium Blend)
recipes.description: A premium bath powder using the same equal-parts soap + borax base as pd-034 but scented with a classic Cologne-water essential oil blend — neroli + rosemary + bergamot + cedrat + orange peel. Spa-luxurious scent profile.
recipes.notes: Sift the soap and borax together. Combine the essential oils in a small dish; drizzle over the powder and stir to distribute. Store in airtight container. The cedrat (Citrus medica) is a citron variety with a distinctive bitter-bright note — substitute lemon peel oil if unavailable.

attribution.displayName: Henley's Twentieth Century Book of Recipes, Formulas and Processes (1907 / 1914 ed.)
attribution.author: Gardner D. Hiscox (ed.)
attribution.originalSource: Henley's — BATH TABLETS, EFFERVESCENT (premium cologne blend variant)
attribution.originalRecipe: For the first quality the following may be taken: Oil of neroli 6 fluidrachms; Oil of rosemary 3 fluidrachms; Oil of bergamot 3 fluidrachms; Oil of cedrat 7 fluidrachms; Oil of orange peel 7 fluidrachms. (Use 1 fluidrachm of this blend per pound of soap/borax base.)
attribution.notes: Henley's described this as the 'first quality' (most expensive) bath powder scent. Suitable for a high-end Sqrrlbrain bundle SKU.

recipes.name: Florida Water
recipes.description: Florida Water — iconic American cologne dating to 1808, still produced today by Murray & Lanman. Citrus-floral-spice blend in alcohol with jasmine and musk essences. Used as a cologne, ritual cleansing water, and freshening splash.
recipes.notes: Combine all ingredients in an amber glass bottle. Shake well. If cloudy, filter through magnesium carbonate. Let mature 2-4 weeks for the scent to fully develop. Apply as cologne or splash. SUBSTITUTION: 'musk essence' historically came from animal sources; modern white-musk synthetic alternatives are widely available from fragrance suppliers and are cruelty-free.

attribution.displayName: Henley's Twentieth Century Book of Recipes, Formulas and Processes (1907 / 1914 ed.)
attribution.author: Gardner D. Hiscox (ed.)
attribution.originalRecipe: Oil of bergamot 3 fluidounces; Oil of lavender 1 fluidounce; Oil of cloves 1 1/4 fluidrachms; Oil of cinnamon 2 1/2 fluidrachms; Oil of neroli 1/2 fluidrachm; Oil of lemon 1 fluidounce; Essence of jasmine 6 fluidounces; Essence of musk 2 fluidounces; Rose water 1 pint; Alcohol 8 pints.
attribution.notes: Florida Water was invented 1808 by Robert I. Murray; Henley's 1907 formula is a faithful period reproduction. Still in commerce today (Murray & Lanman brand). Cross-cultural uses: cologne, ritual cleansing in Latin American/Caribbean spiritualities, after-shave.

recipes.name: Lavender Water (Classic English)
recipes.description: Classic English Lavender Water — the most famous of all perfumed waters. Uses well-matured oil of lavender (Henley's recommends oil aged 5+ years with added rectified spirit). Long maturation produces a smooth, complex lavender cologne.
recipes.notes: Combine all ingredients in an amber bottle. Shake well. CRITICAL: let the perfume stand for at least 1 month before filtering through gray filtering paper or fine coffee filter. The long maturation is what separates a great lavender water from a mediocre one. SUBSTITUTION: ambergris essence is historic/whaling-derived; modern alternatives include synthetic ambergris (Ambroxan, Cetalox) or simple white-musk synthetics — both widely available and cruelty-free.

attribution.displayName: Henley's Twentieth Century Book of Recipes, Formulas and Processes (1907 / 1914 ed.)
attribution.author: Gardner D. Hiscox (ed.)
attribution.originalRecipe: I.— Oil of lavender 1 1/2 ounces; Oil of bergamot 4 drachms; Essence ambergris 4 drachms; Proof spirit 3 pints.
attribution.notes: Henley's quote: 'Some who take pride in this perfume use no oil which is less than 5 years old, and which has had 1 ounce of rectified spirit added to each pound of oil before being set aside to mature.' The 5-year aged lavender is what gives English Lavender Water its character.

recipes.name: Petroleum-Citronella Hair Tonic
recipes.description: An emulsified hair tonic with pale petroleum (light mineral oil), citronella, castor oil, and alcohol. Petroleum delivers slip and shine; citronella adds antimicrobial/insect-repellent action. Distinct from oil-only hair dressings.
recipes.notes: Combine petroleum, citronella, castor oil, and alcohol in a bottle; shake until uniform. Slowly add water with vigorous shaking — the alcohol helps disperse the oils into the water phase. Shake before each use; some separation expected. Apply small amount to scalp; massage in. PRESERVATION: alcohol at 33% is self-preserving.

attribution.displayName: Henley's Twentieth Century Book of Recipes, Formulas and Processes (1907 / 1914 ed.)
attribution.author: Gardner D. Hiscox (ed.)
attribution.originalSource: Henley's — HAIR PREPARATIONS, 'Petroleum Hair Washes I'
attribution.originalRecipe: I.— Deodorized pale petroleum, 10 parts; citronella oil, 10 parts; castor oil, 5 parts; spirit of wine, 90 per cent, 50 parts; water, 75 parts.
attribution.notes: 'Deodorized pale petroleum' = food-grade light mineral oil (USP white mineral oil). Modern equivalent widely available; some 'clean beauty' practitioners avoid mineral oil — substitute fractionated coconut oil for a botanical alternative.

recipes.name: Lemon-Rosemary Hair Oil
recipes.description: An alternate hair oil variant — same sesame/sunflower base as pd-033 but scented bright with lemon, lavender, rosemary, and geranium. Brighter, more invigorating scent profile than the floral-bergamot version.
recipes.notes: Combine all in a bottle; shake. Apply sparingly. The rosemary and lemon combination is associated historically with circulation-stimulating hair tonics. NOTE: lemon oil is photosensitizing — apply at night, or use lemon FCF for daytime use.

attribution.displayName: Henley's Twentieth Century Book of Recipes, Formulas and Processes (1907 / 1914 ed.)
attribution.author: Gardner D. Hiscox (ed.)
attribution.originalSource: Henley's — HAIR PREPARATIONS, 'A Cheap Hair Oil II'
attribution.originalRecipe: II.— Sesame oil or sunflower oil, 1,000 parts; lavender oil, 12 parts; lemon oil, 20 parts; rosemary oil, 5 parts; and geranium oil, 2 parts.
attribution.notes: Companion to pd-033; same base oil, different scent direction. Lemon + rosemary is the classic 'tonic' scent profile in historic hair care.
